QUESTIONS 1 TO 4
01
QUESTION 1

What is it?

Menuverso is the dining club that learns taste. Members pay $9.99 a month or $69.99 a year for member-only offers at restaurants, cafés and bars, ranked by what each member likes. Venues join free and set the offer. Every visit trains the model.

CATEGORY

Subscription dining club, the model The Entertainer has run since 2001 and Neotaste raised a $23M Series A on in 2024, built for the Spanish-speaking world. For a marketer: a channel where the venue's spend is one dish, paid after a confirmed visit.

WHAT A MEMBER GETS

Venues near them, ranked by taste, each with an offer: a 2x1 (buy one, get one) on mains, a free coffee with a cheesecake, $10 off two menus of the day. Pick one, go, show the screen at the table. One use covers the monthly price.

WHAT A VENUE GETS

A free listing, no fee, no commission. A portal to edit or pause the offer. A short video filmed at the venue. Guests it can count.

THE TASTE MODEL

Three levels. A taste profile at sign-up, matched to venues profiled on the same dimensions. Then every redeem, repeat and skip retrains the ranking on what the member does. Then, opt-in, the member's Google Maps history. Level one is in the product. Level two is training on pilot data now.

02
QUESTION 2

Who's the customer, and what do we know that others don't?

The customer is the member. They pay, and every visit they make is a training example. Venues are supply partners and pay nothing. In year two to three a third customer arrives, the buyer of placement and of the aggregate data, and it buys only if the first two keep showing up.

The memberTHE CUSTOMER

Who. A new-gen foodie who goes out several times a week, finds places on short-form video, and arrived through a reel. They decide alone, in the app, in a minute.

Where they go. The most central, easy-to-crave, affordable venues carry most of the confirmed visits. Density gets a member out the door.

Trigger. A venue they already want, near them, with an offer. When we surveyed members who never visited, the most common reason was that nothing convincing was near them.

What we have not profiled yet. Age, income and dining frequency by member. The taste profile at sign-up gives us the dimensions to do it.

The venueSUPPLY · PAYS NOTHING

Who says yes. Independent restaurants, cafés and bars in central Madrid, including the quality tier with 4.5 stars and 300+ reviews. The owner decides, face to face or on WhatsApp. Franchises and large chains are out of scope.

What they are fixing. Reach. Most of our partners have no marketing budget and nobody whose job is marketing. In the US, 46% of operators say advertising is hard.

What they will not do. Pay up front. A free listing, no commission, no hardware and no staff training is what gets the yes.

WHAT A YEAR OF RUNNING IT TAUGHT US
$0.46

Attention is cheap. $0.46 an install and $1.69 a registration from organic reels run as low-budget Meta ads.

80%

Committed members go. Of the roughly 110 members who started a card trial, 80% redeemed within days. The leak is before the trial, and that step is the product work.

0

Staff need nothing. 177 offers redeemed across dozens of venues without a single staff-training problem. No hardware, no integration, no onboarding cost per venue.

2x1

Creative shapes the training set. Deal-first ads bring deal-seekers, and a model trained on deal-seekers learns the price of a burger. The next creative sells discovery, and the taste profile at sign-up makes every member a labelled example from day one.

The other edge is operating history. Patricia ran partner management for Urban Sports Club across 8,000 venues in Spain and Portugal. Rodrigo signed the Madrid venues in person and still sends the outreach from his own phone.
03
QUESTION 3

What's the white space?

Everyone in restaurant discovery ranks on strangers' reviews, because reviews are the data they have. Nobody records what a person chose over the alternatives, went to, and went back to.

That record only exists inside a club that runs the offer at the table. We run it in 130 venues today.

2026
WHAT CHANGED IN DISCOVERY THIS YEAR
12 March

Google launched Ask Maps, a Gemini-powered conversational restaurant search, in the US and India. It personalizes on the places a user has searched and saved.

6 August

Ask Maps began ordering takeout. It builds the cart on the restaurant's own point of sale, Square and Toast first, Uber Eats next, under what Google calls a Universal Commerce Protocol for Food.

The open question

Asked by the AP whether it would sell advertising that improves a business's chance of being recommended, Google did not answer.

Who gets buried

The same coverage lists the failure modes: heavily reviewed places surface over small ones, broad queries favor chains, independents have sparse menus and old photos.

The decision is moving to an assistant that ranks on reviews and search history. Neither knows what anyone ate or whether they went back. The assistant that wins restaurant discovery will need visit data, and the way to have it is to run the visits.

SIX SLICES OF A VISIT

A visit has six moments that matter. Every company below sees some of them. Menuverso is the only row with all six in one person, over months, with consent.

The incumbents are not weak. Each is excellent at its own slice, none has a reason to collect the rest, and the two that see the visit are paid per transaction, so a free membership tier would cut their own revenue line.

WHY IT DOES NOT EXIST YET

The incumbents' revenue lines point the other way. A platform paid per cover or per voucher cannot give a venue a free, repeating member relationship without cutting its own line. A platform paid for attention has no reason to confirm the visit.

The data lives inside the visit. Google sees where people go. Cards see what they spend. OpenTable sees bookings. Which venue a member chose among alternatives, redeemed at, and returned to, with the taste profile behind the choice, is recorded only by whoever runs the offer at the table. Reviews are public and anyone can scrape them. Visits are not.

The likeliest gap-closer is a reservation platform adding a membership tier, or Google selling placement. Both still leave the independent paying per transaction. By then the club holds the taste profiles and visit history in its cities.

The membership model is not new, and that is useful: The Entertainer since 2001, TasteCard since 2006, Neotaste since 2020 in four European markets. None of them operates in Spain or in the US Hispanic metros. We have checked the obvious names and will keep checking.

04
QUESTION 4

Why now, and how big?

1950
THE GAP
Groceries have been measured since the 1980s. Television since 1950. Eating out still runs on surveys and reviews.
MEASURED
Groceries

Scanner panels in a million homes. Every basket, every brand, since the 1980s.

MEASURED
Television

Ratings since 1950. Who watched what, minute by minute.

MEASURED
Retail

Card data by the swipe. Foot traffic by the phone in the pocket.

NOT MEASURED
Eating out

Surveys, scraped menus and reviews. Over a trillion dollars a year in the US alone, and nobody records the visit.

WHY NOW

The decision moved to assistants and short video this year. Ask Maps went live in March and started taking orders in August. 38% of Gen Z find restaurants on TikTok (Toast, October 2025). An independent cannot reach either without budget and skills, and 46% of operators call advertising hard (Toast, 2025). We buy that attention for them at $0.46 an install and hand it back as a visit.

The default is still the familiar. 63% of US diners mostly or always pick a restaurant they already know (Toast, December 2025). An assistant trained on reviews does not change that: ChatGPT recommends 1.2% of chain locations against 35.9% in Google's local pack (SOCi, 2026), and independents less often than chains. A venue-funded offer is what moves a diner off the default.

Subscription data became the ad layer this year, in streaming. Netflix went from 250 million ad viewers to AI-matched creative and ads tuned to viewing behavior in 2026, with ad revenue projected at about $3B. The pattern, subscription first, behavior second, advertising third, is what this club is built to repeat on a smaller and more specific signal: the dinner.

The club model is proven, and the taste layer has never been built on it. Neotaste raised a $23M Series A in 2024 on monthly and yearly dining subscriptions. The Entertainer and TasteCard have run memberships for twenty years. None of them profiles taste or trains on visits. Nobody has built either for the Spanish-speaking world.

HOW BIG · SUBSCRIPTIONS ONLY
$4.5B
TAM. 95M target diners in Spain, US Hispanic hubs and Latin America at about $48 a year.
$1.8B
SAM. 38M diners in launch cities: Spain, US Hispanic hubs, then the top Latin American cities.
$15-29M
SOM, year 3. 300K to 600K members, about 1 to 1.5% of SAM.

The number that matters is the last one. At US pricing of $69.99 a year, 340,000 members is about $24M of subscription revenue. The US Hispanic market alone is 65 million people with $2.5T of annual buying power. Those members are also the training set: 340,000 people making several confirmed visits a month is the dataset no map, card network or review site has, and it is priced by what comparable datasets have sold for, not by this math. That is Question 8b.

THE MESSAGE THAT SIGNS VENUES

Hi {name}! I'm Rodrigo, I run Menuverso, a dining club with about 130 restaurants and 3,000 members in Madrid. I really liked your place and would love to add it to the club. It costs nothing, and we send someone to film a short video of the venue. Interested?

Sent in Spanish, by email, Instagram and WhatsApp. Six lines, no deck, no call. It is how most of the 130 venues were signed.

WHAT RUNS BEHIND IT

A Google Maps scanner runs twice a week across every venue we know in Madrid and flags new openings. New owners are the easiest to sign.

A weekly most-wanted list of venues with 4.5 stars and 300+ reviews.

An Instagram drip in small random batches so the account is never flagged. WhatsApp goes out by hand from the founder's phone.

Restaurant lead ads on Meta: two short reels aimed at people who manage restaurant pages in central Madrid, a one-tap form, the filmed video as the hook.

A self-serve partner portal where the venue edits, pauses or re-photographs its offer, with a dashboard of offer and customer insights.

06
QUESTION 6

Desired future state

Madrid
AT SATURATION · MONTH 18

A member opens the app anywhere central and finds three places they want tonight within a ten-minute walk, each with an offer. That takes 80 or more partner venues per neighborhood, filled one neighborhood at a time.

A partner sees members every week, runs its offer and frequency from its own portal, and reads a simple report: how many members saw it, chose it, came, came back. No other channel gives an independent that report.

The company target at month 18: 180,000 members (60x today's 3,000), 1,500 partner venues (12x today's 130), a $2M ARR run-rate. Gated on month-6 member retention above 60%, CAC payback under 6 months and venue retention above 90%. Those three numbers decide whether a second city opens.

Miami
SECOND CITY · SERIES A

Miami opens with Madrid's playbook and Madrid's numbers: the Maps scanner, the six-line message, restaurant lead ads, the partner portal, and a dense launch list of central venues before a single member ad runs. US pricing of $9.99 a month and $69.99 a year from day one.

The order is Madrid, then the US, then Latin America. We prove retention in one dense home market, then enter the highest-spend Spanish-speaking market in the world with that proof, before Latin America.

Five years out, the plan is 300,000 to 600,000 members across Spain, the US Hispanic hubs and the top Latin American metros, and in each city a Foodie Psychosphere: how that city eats, by neighborhood, occasion and demographic, built from confirmed visits and licensed to restaurant groups, brands, research firms and the assistants themselves. It holds the one signal none of them collects: what people chose, went to, and went back to, with the taste behind the choice.

THE OBJECTION THAT NEARLY KILLED IT

"No hay sitios que me convenzan cerca de mí."

"There are no places near me that convince me." The most common answer in our survey of members who registered and never went out.

130 venues spread across a city of three million is nobody's neighborhood. We stopped counting venues and started counting venues per neighborhood. It is why the Ask is 1,500 venues in 18 neighborhoods, not 1,500 venues in Madrid.

WHO PAYS FOR THE SECOND MEAL
The venue funds the offerA 2x1 on mains, a free coffee with a cheesecake, $10 off two menus of the day. The venue chooses the offer, the hours and the frequency.
Menuverso pays or charges the venueNothing, either way. No listing fee, no commission.
The venue's cost per confirmed guestThe food cost of one dish, on a table that pays for the first dish, the drinks and everything else. We will measure it with three partners before the interview.
Why it still winsIt picked the offer and the slow hours, it pays only when a guest is at the table, and it keeps the whole first cover. Against a per-cover fee or a 20 to 30% voucher cut, the spend stays inside its own margin. The venues that see members weekly keep their offers running.
MARGIN TRAJECTORY

Gross margin stays near 85%. What moves is contribution, with one input. If the trial-start rate goes from 3.6% to the plan's 20% at the same $1.69 a registration, media per trial starter falls from $47 to about $8.45, and 12-month payback holds at any trial-to-paid above 15%.

THE NAPKIN P&L · A PROJECTION
What $2M ARR requires

At the deck's blended $48 a year, the month-18 target is about 42,000 paying members, 23% of the 180,000 registered. It happens if trial starts reach 30% of registrations and three in four of them pay and stay through month 6. Those two numbers are what the seed is spent on.

The 18-month model

Quarter by quarter: members, paying members, ARR, venues, a team of nine, spend from about $65K to $92K a month. The $1.5M carries 18 months at zero revenue. The Growth Plan accompanies this package.

The $10M EBITDA path

Arithmetic, not a plan: $10M of EBITDA at a 40% margin is $25M of revenue, about 360,000 to 420,000 paying members at $69.99 a year. That sits inside the year-3 range of 300,000 to 600,000. Trial-to-paid decides whether it is a path or a wall.

WHAT THE PILOT DATA SHOWS
The most central, easy-to-crave, affordable venues carry most of the 177 confirmed visits.
Of members who redeemed once, about one in five redeemed again. 18 repeat members out of 87 who visited.
80% of trial starters redeem within days. The commitment step predicts the visit.
Venues that saw members weekly stayed. Venues that saw none left. 25% of pilot venues churned, almost all unseen.
WHAT WE EXPECT, NOT YET MEASURED
Saturating a neighborhood to 80+ venues lifts visits per member. Test: visits per member in the first three dense neighborhoods, before a fourth opens.
Personal recommendations hold month-6 retention above 60%. Test: the first charged cohort, read at seed month 7.
Members who connect friends redeem more often and churn less. Test: friend-connected cohort against the rest, from seed month 4.
A restaurant group pays for a neighborhood report. Test: one pilot, priced, at seed month 18.
SUBSCRIPTION, THEN BEHAVIOR, THEN ADS
Netflix
WATCHING → AD BUSINESS

Sold subscriptions for fifteen years before selling an ad. Now 250 million monthly ad viewers and about $3B of 2026 ad revenue, matched to viewing behavior, including in-market audiences for "dining experiences" inferred from what people watch.

Amazon
BUYING → AD BUSINESS

Purchase history became the targeting layer other platforms rent. Since March 2026, Netflix campaigns can target on Amazon's shopping signals.

Menuverso
EATING OUT → AD BUSINESS

The subscription builds the behavior: what each member chose, visited and returned to, with the taste profile behind it. Netflix infers a dining audience from what people watch. We have the dinner. Venues and brands target segments defined by how people eat, and pay on the visit.

Segments are aggregate and anonymized. No individual profile is sold, and nothing is shared without the member's opt-in.

IP
THE FOODIE PSYCHOSPHERE · WHO BUYS IT
Four questions nobody can answer today. Each one is a product the moment the model can.
RESTAURANT GROUP

Which of our three candidate sites in Madrid will fill on weeknights, and with what menu?

Site and concept reports. Placer.ai sells the foot traffic half of this at $100M ARR.

DRINKS OR FOOD BRAND

Which 200 bars should we be poured in, and what gets a 28-year-old to order us the first time?

Occasion and trigger data, and the placement to act on it. Fetch and Numerator sell the receipt half of this.

RESEARCH FIRM

How does a city's taste shift by neighborhood, occasion and age, month over month, from visits rather than surveys?

Panel licensing. Kantar, NIQ, Circana and Ipsos buy behavior panels today.

AI ASSISTANT OR MAPS

What does this person want tonight, within a ten-minute walk, that they would never have found alone?

The recommendation layer itself. Google pays Reddit about $60M a year for human behavior data. Nobody has visit data to sell.

What is licensed is aggregated by city, neighborhood, occasion and demographic. Opt-in, revocable, anonymized. The first data pilot, one restaurant group, one neighborhood report, is in the plan at quarter six.

09
QUESTION 9

What's the wedge, and how does the model resolve?

The wedge

What we charge while we prove it. The Madrid membership, after a 30-day trial, at local pricing below the US list. Venues, nothing.

Time to value. Days. 80% of trial starters redeem within days, and a venue sees value at its first confirmed guest.

Revenue it generates. None yet. The wedge's job is to prove the trial-start rate and retention that set the US numbers. The first billed cohort is the first result the seed buys.

Closed doors
ONE THING WE DO, FOUR WE DO NOT

Scaling consumer ads before activation moves. Top of funnel is solved. Buying members who do not go out is wasted media.

Franchises and large chains. Out of scope. Independent groups of two to six venues are in.

A second city on the seed. Madrid until the three gates clear. Miami on the Series A.

Charging venues. Closed until the density loop turns. Restaurants list free. Revenue comes from member subscriptions.

WHAT STOPS THEFORK OR GOOGLE COPYING IT
IF THEY TRIEDWHAT THEY SEE OF A VISITWHAT THEY WOULD HAVE TO GIVE UP
TheFork, OpenTableTwo of six slices: the booking and the seat. Bookable venues only, which leaves out most bars, cafés and the walk-in independents that make up the club.The per-cover fee. A free membership tier that sends diners to venues without a booking cuts the line they are paid on.
GoogleThree of six: searches, inferred location, repeat location. Never the taste behind the choice, never the offer that moved it, never a confirmed table.Neutrality. Running member offers at the table means picking venues, which an advertising marketplace cannot be seen to do.
Card networksThree of six: merchant, spend, repeat spend. No taste, no alternatives considered, no offer.Nothing structural. They lack the consumer relationship and the venue relationship. They are a buyer of this data, not a builder.
A new dining clubCould build the same six slices from zero.Time. Density is built one neighborhood at a time, and the model is only as good as the months of visits behind it. By the Series A, Madrid is 18 months ahead.
STICKINESS

Unknown. No paid cohort has reached month 6. The gates are month-6 member retention above 60% and venue retention above 90%. The first billed members and the 130 live venues are the cohorts that answer.

HOW THE MODEL RESOLVES

Per member, gross-profitable from the first payment. At company level the proof period is funded by the seed: $1.5M for 18 months in Madrid, in three $500K tranches on post-money SAFEs with the cap stepping from $6M to $9M, then US pricing from Miami on the Series A. We have not modeled break-even past month 18, which is why Question 11 asks for help there.

5Y
FIVE YEARS

The dining club of the Spanish-speaking world: 300,000 to 600,000 members across Spain, the US Hispanic hubs and the top Latin American metros, and in every city a Foodie Psychosphere built from confirmed visits. Venues stay because members come weekly. Placement is sold on the visit. Groups, research firms and the assistants license the city model because no other source records the visit together with the taste behind it.

WHAT WE HEARD, WHAT WE CHANGED
"Nothing convincing near me," from members who never visited. We changed the opening rule: a neighborhood opens only with a dense cluster of venues in one central area, and we built the weekly list of 4.5-star, 300-review venues to go after.
Venue signings depended on someone being paid to sign them. We built automated sourcing, the six-line message, and restaurant lead ads with the filming hook, the first cold channel that signs venues.
Most registered members never started a trial. We moved to a 30-day trial and made the share of new members who visit within 14 days the one number the company steers by. Paid acquisition does not scale until it moves.
Most partners had no working website. We built a script that turns a venue's Maps listing into a website with bookings in seconds, with a person checking every price. Free for partners.
WHO FOLLOWED

The first 130 venues signed on a founder's word, before there was a video, a dashboard or a case study. A freelance developer and two content interns have worked with us before there was money to pay market rates. Three of them will join the first conversation.

WHAT HAS TO BE TRUE IN YEAR FIVE

That a member in Madrid or Miami opens the app on a Tuesday and finds somewhere they did not know, goes, and tells a friend. Every one of those visits teaches the model something. If that stops happening, the Foodie Psychosphere is worth nothing and I would not want to sell it anyway.

That venues stay because members come, not because we gave them a free website. The day our retention tool is a tool and not a guest, we have built restaurant software.

That the company is American with Spanish roots, run from the US, with the first city still alive and still ours. I have launched four markets for other people. This is the one I keep.

THE THING I LEAST WANT TO TELL YOU

Of 3,000 people who registered, about 110 ever started a trial. We acquired cheaply and watched 96 in 100 do nothing, and for most of the year we called the top of the funnel a success.

The second thing: our first year of members came for a deal. The taste model needs people who come for discovery. If the same ads cannot bring both, the acquisition cost in Question 8 is the wrong number.

11
QUESTION 11

Why build this with Gateway X?

Because the model is only as good as the visits that train it, and getting members to the table is an acquisition problem. Gateway X was built by people who do customer acquisition for a living. Five requests, each tied to something you already do.

01
Move one number

We buy a registered member for $1.69 and 3.6% start a trial. We want your funnel discipline on that step: creative that sells discovery over the deal, onboarding that puts the offer before the paywall, and experiment design that tells us in weeks what moved it.

02
Your playbooks, applied

Your mutual-intro scripts and relationship CRM, run against the 18 Madrid restaurant groups we have mapped and not signed. Your 833 calculator and 12-month P&L model on our wedge.

03
Hands for the tests

Aux launched through GX's network with GrowthAssistant contractors. We want the same: contractor capacity for creative variants, lead-ad operations and the twenty customer conversations, so two founders are not the bottleneck on learning.

04
An operating scorecard

The pilot has no retention cohort, no trial-to-paid number and no exit interviews. We want your standard for data hygiene and a weekly scorecard for a two-sided club, in place before the seed is spent.

05
The first data buyer

Our plan is venture-shaped. Yours is not. We want the version of this wedge that pays for itself per neighborhood, and help designing the first Foodie Psychosphere product, one restaurant group, one neighborhood report, sold inside the fellowship, so the data layer has a customer before the Series A.

WHAT WE BRING

A live two-sided product with a year of data. A founder who has built and sold this shape of business and run its partner side at 8,000 venues. A cofounder who signs restaurants himself. A market no US dining club serves. And a dataset the discovery stack does not produce: confirmed visits, with the taste behind them.
